papers.title: Tokamak-SI: Interpreting Tokamak Discharges with Labeled Catalogs
papers.abstract: Finding which phenomena occur in a tokamak discharge, and when, is often a manual task. Previous efforts at labeling events have been task-specific, each with its own corpus of data. We introduce Tokamak-SI, which combines the labels and labeling methods of many earlier studies into a single scalable, time-aligned, and categorical dataset covering observations from confinement, detachment, alfven eigenmodes (AE), edge localized modes (ELM), sawtooth, tearing modes (TM), and resistive wall modes in DIII-D tokamak. Models based on this, which can extend the labels to new shots, match or beat earlier detectors on its labels, including for AE, ELM, and TM detection. Tokamak-SI is intended to enable task-specific benchmarking, physics-searchable archives, and direct identification of key events during an experiment.

papers.title: Effects of Alfv\'enicity on the Compressible Energy Cascade in Magnetohydrodynamic Solar Wind Turbulence: Evidence from Parker Solar Probe, Solar Orbiter, and WIND observations
papers.abstract: The compressible MHD energy cascade in the solar wind is shaped by Alfv\'enicity, plasma fluctuations, and proton temperature, yet how these factors regulate the relative weight of compressible and incompressible energy transfer across heliocentric distances remains poorly understood. We apply compressible and incompressible exact relations to a large sample of 2-hour intervals from WIND (1~au), Parker Solar Probe ($<0.25$~au), and Solar Orbiter (0.3--1~au), classifying intervals as Alfv\'enic ($|\sigma_c|>0.75$) or non-Alfv\'enic ($|\sigma_c|<0.25$) and by wind speed, and examine the Yaglom-like and purely compressible components of the compressible cascade. Velocity fluctuation amplitude is the strongest predictor of the compressible cascade rate $\langle|\varepsilon_c|\rangle$, followed by density and magnetic field fluctuations. $\langle|\varepsilon_c|\rangle$ and $\langle|\varepsilon_i|\rangle$ are tightly correlated in all regimes, with their ratio organized by Alfv\'enicity and wind speed: non-Alfv\'enic and Alfv\'enic fast winds cluster along $\langle|\varepsilon_c|\rangle=\langle|\varepsilon_i|\rangle$, while Alfv\'enic slow wind shows a systematic excess consistent with internal energy contributions. The largest $\langle|\varepsilon_c|\rangle$ systematically occur in hotter intervals, with a two-decade increase from cool to hot events in Alfv\'enic slow and non-Alfv\'enic wind, a trend carried mainly by the purely compressible term, while the dominant Yaglom-like term controls the overall cascade magnitude. Alfv\'enicity and wind speed thus govern the efficiency of turbulent energy transfer across heliocentric distances, and the tight coupling between compressible and incompressible rates points to the need for compressible, multi-fluid descriptions of the solar wind dissipation budget.

papers.title: Scaling the Wavelength to Optimize Ultrafast Laser Processing of Bandgap Materials
papers.abstract: The spectral characteristics of ultrashort laser pulses offer unique possibilities to control interactions in space and time as well as the subsequent material responses. In particular, selecting the wavelength predefines the fundamental mechanisms governing laser-matter interaction, and thus, how energy is deposited. This Chapter provides an overview on how the essential physical effects in ultrafast laser-matter interaction scale with the wavelength, and the consequences for bandgap material processing applications. First, we recall the main spectral properties of bandgap materials and discuss the important question of the expected processing resolutions depending on wavelength. Then, recent studies on the impact of the wavelength in ultrafast laser-dielectric interaction are presented. Finally, we present how the latest developments in infrared ultrafast laser sources can be advantageously utilized to internally process narrow-gap materials despite challenges related to increased nonlinearities.

papers.title: Plasma morphology under nanosecond repetitively pulsed discharges with air cross-flow: A simulation study
papers.abstract: Nanosecond repetitively pulsed discharges in air cross-flows exhibit distinct plasma morphologies that can expand the spatial extent of bulk plasma regions and increase the residence time of reactive radicals within the flow field. This work develops a high-fidelity plasma-fluid simulation framework within OpenFOAM that couples drift-diffusion-convection transport, electrostatic potential, photoionization, mixture-averaged transport, ambipolar diffusion, and a local mean electron energy formulation. Using this framework, we systematically investigate plasma morphologies under air cross-flow velocities of 40 and 100 m/s at a repetition frequency of 50 kHz. The simulations show that lower cross-flow velocities promote plasma retention within previously formed channels, resulting in substantial thermal accumulation. In contrast, at higher cross-flow velocities, plasma is rapidly convected downstream, reducing retention between pulses and weakening thermal accumulation. The simulations further reveal the mechanisms responsible for snap-back, in which a subsequent discharge shifts from a previously formed channel to a shorter and more direct path between the electrodes as the conductivity of the previous channel decreases. As a strong electric field develops between the electrodes, electrons are accelerated and intense Joule heating occurs near the anode tip. This process increases the local electron energy, enhances electron production, and generates a stronger discharge current. As the conductivity of the previous channel decreases, the discharge consequently establishes a new path of least resistance directly between the electrodes.

papers.title: Overview of Enhanced D-alpha and Quasi Continuous Exhaust H-modes at DIII-D
papers.abstract: We review the Enhanced D-alpha (EDA) and Quasi-continuous Exhaust (QCE) H-modes that have recently been achieved in the DIII-D tokamak. These scenarios are free of large type-I edge-localized modes (ELMs) and achieved at high fueling compatible with divertor detachment. This makes them promising operational regimes as ELMs are a major risk for fusion pilot plants (FPPs). Access to EDA H-mode and the associated quasi-coherent mode (QCM) was observed at low heating power barely above the L-H power threshold, and increased density enabled access to EDA H-mode even at higher heating powers. The QCE H-mode was achieved at simultaneously high density and heating power, characterized also by a QCM and small ELMs with transient peaks of the total power into the divertor below about 3MW, in line with observations at ASDEX Upgrade. During the QCE H-mode, the turbulence parameter alpha_t at the separatrix is about 1 and does not separate ELMy or EDA from QCE H-modes well. Peeling ballooning stability calculations suggest that the EDA H-mode pedestal is limited by transport far away from ideal magnetohydrodynamic instability, and the QCE H-mode pedestal operates close to the ballooning branch of the stability boundary. BOUT++ simulations qualitatively reproduce the pressure collapse characteristics of the different regimes and suggest an important role of n ~ 50 resistive ballooning modes localized near the separatrix at the X-point during EDA and QCE H-modes. This work provides a foundation and guidance for further research on the access conditions and physics mechanisms of EDA and QCE H-modes necessary for the extrapolation of these regimes towards an FPP.

papers.title: Two-component Bayesian modeling in the data analysis of collective Thomson scattering
papers.abstract: We apply Bayesian inference to the analysis of collective Thomson scattering (CTS) spectra, a diagnostic technique for determining local plasma parameters. Using the population annealing Monte Carlo (PAMC) method, we evaluate the posterior probability density functions (PDFs) for six plasma parameters. The analysis is performed separately for the ion acoustic wave (IAW) and electron plasma wave (EPW) features and jointly for both features. The results show that the combined analysis provides constraints on all six parameters, although the degree of constraint depends on the parameter, whereas the separate analyses provide strong constraints only on complementary subsets of the parameters. In particular, the combined analysis provides a clear constraint on the ion charge state, which is not determined by either separate analysis alone. These findings demonstrate the importance of Bayesian modeling that accounts for the two-component nature of plasmas, consisting of ions and electrons.

papers.title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: delocalization length for heat-flux
papers.abstract: The delocalization length $\lambda_d=\lambda_{ei} Z/\sqrt{Z+4.45}$ is an improved heat-flux non-locality metric accounting for the localizing effect of electron-electron collisions on the electron population carrying heat-flux. Magnetization also localizes the carrier electrons; the delocalization Hall parameter $\psi_d=13.5 \chi Z/(Z+4.62)$ shows that this occurs at a faster rate than magnetization of thermal conductivity ($\psi_{\kappa}= 9.94\chi(Z+0.17)/(Z+5.88)$). The traditional Knudsen number, which uses the electron-ion mean-free path, does not fairly represent non-locality across ionization and magnetization; $Kn_d = 8.28\lambda_{d\bot}/L_T$ should instead be used. The kinetic understanding of the three magnetized heat-flux components is unified in the linear regime with a full electron-electron collision operator and a converged harmonic expansion of the electron distribution (up to $f_6$). Righi-Leduc heat-flux is found to delocalize easier than its perpendicular counterpart, due to its carriers being higher energy electrons. This approach lays the groundwork for a consistent treatment of the kinetically-modified induction equation.

papers.title: Predicting Negative Triangularity Edge Confinement with a Neutral-Coupled Full-f Gyrokinetic Model
papers.abstract: Global full-f gyrokinetic simulations coupled to a reduced neutral-fluid model reproduce key DIII-D experimental trends and identify mechanisms underlying improved confinement in negative triangularity (NT) configurations relative to positive triangularity (PT). Using Gkeyll, we simulate DIII-D inner-wall-limited discharges across the confined edge, scrape-off layer (SOL), and sheath boundaries, allowing the edge electric field to evolve self-consistently. Compared with an adaptive recycling-source model, the reduced neutral fluid model improves particle and energy balances and brings the simulated density and temperature profiles into closer agreement with measurements, with minimal additional computational cost. In NT, suppressed turbulent fluxes coincide with a broad, stationary zonal flow inside the last closed flux surface, whereas PT develops transient, fragmented shear layers. Spectral analysis indicates that modified fluctuation phase relationships and enhanced zonal shear both contribute to transport suppression despite broadly comparable fluctuation amplitudes. The larger co-current departure from a locally matched bi-Maxwellian in NT suggests a velocity-selective kinetic process that may help establish the edge radial electric field by modifying flows or current balance. These results identify kinetic and turbulent mechanisms associated with improved NT confinement within an experimentally established ELM-free regime and demonstrate the importance of coupling gyrokinetic plasma dynamics with neutral interactions across the confined plasma and SOL.

papers.title: A Multiscale Eulerian Vlasov-Rosenbluth-Fokker-Planck Algorithm for Thermonuclear Burning Plasmas
papers.abstract: Accurate treatment of energetic fusion byproducts in laboratory plasmas often requires a kinetic description, owing to their large birth kinetic energy and long mean free paths compared with the characteristic system scale lengths. For example, alpha particles produced by deuterium-tritium fusion reactions are born at high energies (\qty{3.5}{MeV}) and predominantly slow down through interactions with electrons traveling at comparable speeds. As an alpha particle slows, its distribution collapses near the background ion-thermal speed, forming a sharp structure in velocity space. Such sharp features pose numerical challenges in grid-based Eulerian methods: capturing the full alpha-particle energies demands a large velocity domain, while resolving the near-thermal region requires a sufficiently fine mesh. Inspired by the work of Peigney \textit{et al.}~[\textit{J.\ Comput.\ Phys.} \textbf{278} (2014)], we present a two-grid approach that splits the alpha-particle distribution into energetic (suprathermal) and ash (thermal) components. A Gaussian-based sink term transfers particles from the energetic population to the ash population as they slow to the thermal regime, and a conservative projection scheme ensures that mass, momentum, and energy of the slowing energetic alpha population are conserved when it is remapped onto the ash grid. Unlike the formulation of Peigney \textit{et al.}, our method does not require a strict asymptotic separation of velocity scales, which can, in principle, be arbitrary. We demonstrate the robustness of this approach on challenging multiscale problems, including a surrogate for an igniting inertial confinement fusion capsule.

papers.title: ModeCast: One-Shot Prediction of Linear MHD Eigenmodes and Growth Rates in Tokamaks
papers.abstract: Large-scale magnetohydrodynamic instabilities break plasma confinement, can trigger disruptions, and constrain fusion reactor design; modeling a single configuration against them takes hours with a reference solver such as JOREK, and a design study requires thousands of hours. ModeCast is the first learned surrogate to return the complete linear stability assessment for MHD modes. Trained on a comprehensive dataset of over 45,000 JOREK simulations across thousands of equilibria, it screens stability across toroidal mode numbers n=1-4 and predicts the full spatial structure and growth rate of unstable modes. With a second network of the same architecture replacing the equilibrium solve, the full pipeline from design parameters runs on one GPU up to 1,000,000x faster than JOREK's equilibrium and linear stability runs. The gain comes from building the linear-phase physics into the formulation, objective, and inputs, yielding up to six times more training data. ModeCast misses none of the unstable held-out cases, and its predicted fields reproduce the simulation's measured physics, from magnetic island topology to resistivity trends. On a fixed-geometry resistivity scan outside its training distribution, refitting only the 22k-parameter growth rate head of the 145M-parameter network on four simulation halves the held-out internal kink growth rate error, and fine-tuning the whole network adds little. Because it is differentiable and returns full fields, ModeCast could in the future assimilate experimental measurements, providing a bridge to real devices and accelerating progress toward commercial fusion. Project page: zenithon.ai/research/modecast.
